To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

mercury resistance plasmid diversity was observed in the rhizosphere and phyllosphere of sugar beets in three successive years, and that the plasmid groups identified are established in this environment.

(i) mercury resistance plasmid groups have been isolated from sugar beet in three consecutive years; (ii) these plasmids have undergone structural changes; (iii) the frequency of exogenous plasmid isolation correlates with the physiological status of donors prior to plasmid sampling; (iv) the plasmid groups isolated in consecutive years were different from each other and from plasmids obtained from other sources.
In summary, our research is concerned with
plasmid transfer in the rhizosphere and the persistence of mercury resistant plasmid structural groups in a natural habitat.
the isolation and identification of mercury resistance plas- mids, which may have potential for biotechnological use.
the diversity of mercury resistance plsmids in the bacterial communities of sugar beet.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the plasmids were not mobile in the environment and were not involved in the transfer of antibiotic resistance.
mercury resistance plasmid diversity is not influenced by the physiological state of the donor prior to sampling, but by the factors likely to influence bacterial activity and plant growth.
the diversity of plasmids obtained from the bacteria of the sugar beet rhizoplane and phyllosphere is low, but that this low diversity has persisted over three consecutive years.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the mercury resistance determinants in the plasmids are likely to be the most stable genetic elements in the rhizosphere and phyllosphere of sugar beet, and that the mercury resistance plasmid groups are stable over time.
the mercury resistance plasmid diversity in sugar beet is relatively low, with a few plasmid groups persisting in the bacterial population over time.
mercury resistance plasmid diversity is influenced by the plant growth conditions, bacterial activity and donor physiological state at the time of isolation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the diversity of plasmids is not static and is subject to change over time, even in a relatively stable environment such as a crop field.
plasmids can be exogenously isolated over a number of years from a given habitat, and that this is a reliable method for obtaining plasmids that can be used for genetic engineering.
the mercury resistance plasmid groups identified in the present study have been maintained in the sugar beet rhizosphere and phyllosphere over three consecutive years.
